title: No such thing as a dangerous lift (the good morning example)
summary: Using the good morning as his example, NH argues that lifts aren't good or bad in themselves: each sits on a 'totem pole' of risk versus reward, and danger depends on how you apply it. He explains his good morning (45 degrees, knee bend, SSB) and why locked-knee hinges are pointless, and lists technique, load, cumulative fatigue across sessions and leverage as the real risk factors. He defends the behind-the-neck press as no more dangerous than a squat grip.
claims: There's no such thing as bodybuilder form or powerlifter form, only form; any lift can serve size or strength
The good morning is dangerous in the sense of high risk and high reward, not a lift to avoid; the danger comes from how people use it
Good mornings carry over to both squat and deadlift, mostly by building rigidity through the lumbar and thoracic spine
Lifts fail when form breaks down first; if you can do good mornings every week for years without injury, your squat and deadlift injury risk drops
The red zone, where the lift reverses from lowering to lifting, is where injuries happen; on a good morning it falls at the weakest near-horizontal position, with no easy bail-out
Good mornings sit at the very top of the danger totem pole: failing pulls you into loaded lumbar flexion
He does good mornings only to about 45 degrees with a knee bend, matching his torso angle in the squat and deadlift for specificity
Going horizontal on a risky lift like the good morning forces you to use baby weight and defeats the purpose
He recommends doing good mornings with a safety squat bar
Stiff-leg deadlifts and good mornings with locked knees are pointless; some knee bend adds quad and posterior-chain involvement and spares the lumbar spine
No commonly programmed lift is bad for everyone, only bad for you or done badly by you; that's personal responsibility
If a lift keeps hurting after a fair try, replace it; ten other lifts do the same job, and bodybuilders aren't obliged to do any particular lift
Visual cues can't judge form or danger; fearing what looks dangerous is how non-lifters view squats and deadlifts
A rounded lower back on maximal deadlifts is broadly bad unless you're chasing a competition PR
Judge a lift's danger by the stress and fatigue it creates, inside and outside the workout; joint or tendon damage the next day makes it bad even if it felt fine
Stimulus and fatigue are the same thing seen positively or negatively
Isolation lifts injure fewer joints and the damage is localised; compounds like the squat can hurt the lower back (most common), knees and hips
Isolation injuries aren't necessarily milder; some last months while some deadlift tweaks heal in two weeks
High-danger lifts should open the workout, when you're fresh and focused
Most injuries happen when you're on autopilot and not mentally present during the set
Both extremes are wrong: the 'form police' who demand one way, and those who claim technique doesn't matter
Load sets the stress of a lift; exceeding what you can handle causes injury, so program loads properly
Injuries often come from fatigue accumulated over previous sessions rather than what you did that day
Seek neither only weak nor only strong positions; find the setup that moves the most weight with proper form across a given range
For hypertrophy, choose the technique that lets you accumulate the most tonnage safely over time, even if its 1RM is lower
The behind-the-neck press uses the same shoulder position as gripping a low-bar squat; it's fine within your own pain-free range
Old powerlifters' shoulder problems that stop them squatting with a close grip mostly come from benching
Natural doesn't mean optimal; a fully rounded spine is natural but a weak, compromised position
Evaluate every lift by what it feeds, the tonnage it gives, and the risk if you fail
exercises: stop at ~45 degrees, slight knee bend, preferably SSB bar
carries over to squat and deadlift via spinal rigidity; high risk/high reward
locked knees overload lumbar spine without extra muscle recruitment
example of a strong position that allows more weight than a deadlift
find your own range; don't go too deep into shoulder flexion
same shoulder position as squat grip; unfairly vilified
